tracks.title: Plans that run
tracks.text: Lesson eight — workflows. A workflow is a plan written in the grammar. Tasks, states, dependencies, and schedules… in one parseable file. Boards render from it. Agents execute from it. [curious] And nothing ever needs syncing — because the plan is the state.

tracks.title: The plan is always stale
tracks.text: Every project keeps a plan… and almost no project keeps it where the work happens. The board lives in one tool. The code in another. The schedule in a third. And the moment work moves, the plan is a screenshot of last week's intentions. [sighs] Someone's job quietly becomes updating the board. Which is to say… manually syncing reality into a database that only drifts away from it again. The deep cause isn't laziness. It's architecture. A tracker is a second system of record — the work has one state, the plan has another, and nothing structural connects them. Every standup where someone reads the board aloud, and someone else corrects it from memory… is the interest payment on that split. [curious] And agents made this worse before they made it better. An agent's plan typically lives in its context window. Invisible… unreviewable… gone when the session ends. The most plan-hungry collaborators we've ever had arrived… and we gave them the one format nothing else can read.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A workflow is a plan written in the grammar. Tasks, states, dependencies, and schedules, in one parseable file — which boards render from… and agents execute from. The whole trick is in those two verbs. Nothing renders to a workflow, and nothing exports from it. The file is the single source. Everything else is a view, or a worker. Change the file… and every board updates. Finish a task… and the file says so. There is no second copy to keep honest. And a real one is small enough to say out loud. Five headlines. Ship the landing page… write copy, already done… render hero art… build page, which depends on hero art… and deploy — scheduled for Friday morning, depending on build. And under deploy, one line of plain prose: waiting on the brand pass… see thread with m. The reason lives exactly where the waiting happens — not in a comment thread three tools away.

tracks.title: What a plan can say
tracks.text: Because workflows are written in org, the things a plan needs are native grammar — not bolted-on convention. Five of them. First: states. The TODO and DONE keywords on headlines… the board columns, living in the file. Second: dependencies. A property on the task — and execution order falls out of them, never written down. Third: schedules. Real timestamps — so calendars and overdue checks become arithmetic. Fourth: prose. The why, in full sentences, exactly where the decision lives. And fifth: nesting. Workflows hold sub-workflows… a quarter holds projects, holds tasks. One tree. [curious] And the quiet property that matters most — every line of it is parseable. Duplicated tasks… dependencies pointing at nothing… a DONE resting on a TODO. Those are checkable facts. A test suite can read your plan.

tracks.title: The ready set
tracks.text: The ready set. All of workflow execution rests on one tiny definition… so let's give it the space it deserves. A task is ready when two things are true. It's still TODO… and every task it depends on is DONE. That's it. No priorities engine. No scheduler config. Readiness is a fact you can compute by reading the file. Now picture the landing-page plan as the dependency graph the kernel sees. Four tasks. Write copy floats off to the side, already done — it never blocked anything. Render hero art is lit up green — ready, right now. Build page waits on hero art. And deploy waits on build. One finished task… one ready task… and a chain of two behind it. Two things jump out of that picture. First — copy was never in the critical path at all. It ran whenever someone had a free hour… and plans are full of work like that. The graph finds it for you. And second — nobody ever drew that graph. It's computed from the dependency properties, every time, from the current state of the file. When the file changes, the graph changes. [chuckles] There is nothing to keep in sync… because there is only one artifact.

tracks.title: Watching a board clear
tracks.text: Execution is a loop so simple it barely deserves the name. Find the ready set… do it… write DONE back… repeat. Each pass is a round — so watch the landing-page board clear in three. Round one: hero art goes DONE… and build unblocks. Round two: build page goes DONE… and deploy unblocks, holding for its nine o'clock. Round three: deploy goes DONE. Board clear — every state written in the file. Notice what nobody wrote — an execution order. The order fell out of the dependencies. Reorder the headlines, and nothing changes. Add a dependency, and everything downstream waits. And notice who the workers are… the loop doesn't care. A human working down the ready list, and an agent on a schedule, are interchangeable at this seam. The agent finishes round one overnight. You pick up round two with your coffee. [chuckles] The file is the meeting. And when the ready set is empty but TODOs remain… the board is stuck. Stuckness is diagnosable — the only thing that blocks a task is a named dependency. The answer to why-is-this-not-moving is a path through the graph… not an archaeology project.

tracks.title: Boards are renderings
tracks.text: A kanban board. A timeline. A calendar of deadlines. In this ecosystem, those are renderings of the plan file — generated the way a browser generates a page from HTML. Drag a card to the done column… and the file's headline flips to DONE. Edit the file… and the board redraws. [chuckles] The two can't disagree. Because there aren't two. And a board that's secretly a text file inherits everything text already has. The plan gets code review. The plan has a diff. The plan can be reverted… blamed… branched… and merged. [excited] Six months from now, why-did-we-descope-search is answered by the plan's git log. The archaeology is already done.

tracks.title: Time is native
tracks.text: There's a third place plans secretly live — after the board and the tracker. The cron job. That other system where what-should-happen-and-when sits, readable by exactly one daemon, and reviewed by no one. Workflows absorb it. Scheduled and deadline are timestamps on the headline itself… so the temporal half of a plan sits in the same parseable tree as the structural half. Publish the changelog, every Friday morning — that's a property on a task, not a line in a crontab. [curious] On a docked workbook, the engine fires these. And a passed deadline on a TODO is a fact the validator reports… not a notification you missed. The task's history accumulates under the same headline — so when-did-this-last-run is a read, not an investigation.

tracks.title: Plans hold plans
tracks.text: Plans hold plans. Headlines nest… so plans do. Picture one tree. At the top, the quarter. Inside it, two projects — ship the landing page… and launch the CLI. And inside each of those, the tasks — copy done over here, a docs pass waiting over there. The same readiness rule runs at every level — a parent is done when its children are. One tree carries the whole altitude range, from the big quarterly bets… down to rename-that-variable. This sounds like a small convenience until you've lived the alternative. The roadmap in a slide deck. The projects in a tracker. The tasks in fifteen heads. Here, the altitudes are the same document at different depths. Zoom out for the quarter… zoom in for the work. And the rollup percentages are queries… not status meetings.

tracks.title: The compile story
tracks.text: The compile story — a depth rung, skippable… but it's where workflows stop being a productivity feature and become infrastructure. The engine reads the same shape, one level deeper. A workflow whose tasks are tagged as components — each carrying a source block, with declared inputs and outputs — compiles into a world. A deployable unit, whose data-flow edges are computed by matching one component's output to another's input. Picture the smallest one. A plan with two component tasks: render, which outputs a page… and publish, which takes a page in, and puts a site out. The kernel tangles the plan — matches render's output to publish's input — and out comes a world, with that one edge drawn for you… exporting the site. Same grammar. Same file. Same validator. The conceptual rhyme is the point. A to-do list and a build system are the same data structure — tasks, with dependencies — and the ecosystem refuses to make you learn them twice. From sticky-note scale… to build-system scale… it's one idea, wearing different clothes.

tracks.title: What it replaces
tracks.text: So what does this replace? Honestly… parts of three things. The tracker holds states, but the plan lives in someone else's cloud, agents read it lossily through an API, and there's no diff. The CI pipeline executes and lives beside the code… but it only fires on push, and it has no states and no prose. And cron knows about time… and nothing else, invisibly. [curious] A workflow is what you get when the tracker's states, the pipeline's execution, and cron's sense of time agree to live in one reviewable file. Each of those tools still exists for a reason — at the boundary of your system, you'll meet all three. Inside it… you stop needing them to agree with each other. Because they're reading the same plan.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Honesty section. Plans drift. Agents writing freely will eventually duplicate a task, or contradict a state — and a workflow file doesn't prevent that, any more than any format does. What it does is make drift detectable. The checks run on every write… and the contradiction gets a name and a line number, instead of a shrug. Dependency graphs have failure modes of their own. Cycles deadlock a board — the validator catches them before anything runs, but you still have to decide which edge was wrong. And over-specified dependencies are the quiet killer. [chuckles] Declare everything-depends-on-everything… and you've serialized your team. The graph executes whatever truth you write. Writing less of it is sometimes the optimization. And execution is not autonomy. The pitch is never software that runs itself. Direction stays human… workers stop at the edges you set… and the edges are real. [curious] A workflow makes follow-through cheap. It doesn't make judgment optional.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] How is this different from Jira, or Linear? Those are databases with views — the plan lives in their cloud, in their shape. A workflow lives next to the work, in plain text, in version control. [chuckles] Use both if you like… only one of them can be diffed in a pull request. What stops circular dependencies? Validation — a cycle, a phantom dependency, a DONE resting on a TODO, each reported and named before anything runs. Who executes the tasks? Anyone who can read the file. You… an agent on a schedule… a fleet of them on an engine. Does my whole team need to read org? No — that's what renderings are for. The board is the interface most people touch. The file is what it's made of. [curious] And… is the Autopoet one of these? Exactly one of these. A standing agent, working a maintenance workflow against the system itself. It's the worked example of this whole lesson… and it has its own sub-lesson.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: So that's a workflow. One parseable plan — boards render from it, agents execute from it, time is native, and the order falls out of the dependencies. [curious] If you want to see one tending a real system, the Autopoet sub-lesson is next door. Otherwise… the place all of this work actually lives is the next lesson. The disk that rides in the file. The VFS.
